title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: “Working capital absorbed Rs 300.3 crore during the year.”
epigraph.author: Financial Express, standalone FY2026 [24]

web_blocks.html: The sources read do not describe distributors or resellers. The company sells qualified parts directly to OEMs and to large project buyers such as BHEL [35], and export revenue was about 92% of FY2025 sales [31]. For this business the distribution question is less about reaching customers than about keeping a qualified place in each customer’s programme and collecting the cash that programme generates.

The waterfall below uses the consolidated annual snapshot for FY2026, so every row describes the same fiscal year and no trailing figures are mixed in. It is scaled to ₹100 of revenue so the reader can see what each rupee of sales left behind.

web_blocks.caption: AZAD: FY2026 revenue-to-cash waterfall, consolidated, in ₹ crore and per ₹100 of revenue
web_blocks.takeaway: Every row is scaled to ₹100.00 of FY2026 consolidated sales. Net profit is ₹22.22 per ₹100 of sales, while operating cash flow was negative ₹19.73.

lines.label: Revenue (sales)
lines.note: Consolidated FY2026 sales, the base for every row.

lines.label: Operating expenses
lines.note: Expenses line in the consolidated snapshot.

lines.label: Operating profit
lines.note: Operating profit before other income, interest and depreciation.

lines.label: Depreciation
lines.note: Depreciation in FY2026; it was ₹29 crore in FY2025.

lines.label: Other income
lines.note: Non-operating income, about a quarter of pre-tax profit in this year.

lines.label: Income tax (implied)
lines.note: Profit before tax less net profit; the snapshot gives no separate tax line.

lines.label: Cash flow from operations
lines.note: Operating cash flow for the same fiscal year.

lines.label: Cash flow from investing
lines.note: Investing outflow; the snapshot carries no separate capex line.

web_blocks.html: Read from the top, ₹100 of revenue carried ₹62.69 of operating expenses, leaving ₹37.31 of operating profit. Depreciation took ₹8.79 and interest ₹5.14, while other income added ₹7.63. That leaves ₹31.01 of profit before tax and ₹22.22 of net profit. Operating cash flow was negative ₹19.73 and investing outflow ₹11.77 per ₹100, so the two cash lines together absorbed ₹31.50 of every ₹100 of sales.

The distance between reported profit and cash is the central fact of the year. Net profit of ₹134 crore against operating cash flow of negative ₹119 crore is a gap of ₹253 crore, or ₹41.95 per ₹100 of sales. The sources point to working capital as the absorber. The standalone FY2026 account reports working capital absorbed of ₹300.3 crore [24] and operating cash flow of negative ₹123.3 crore [23]. The consolidated and standalone figures differ by a few crore, and both show the same sign.

Working capital moved further in the first half of FY2027. Inventory rose to ₹424.8 crore at September 2026 from ₹326.6 crore at March 2026 [25], and trade receivables rose to ₹401.6 crore from ₹309.2 crore [26]. Together those two lines added about ₹190 crore in six months. Total borrowings rose from ₹451.6 crore to ₹557.0 crore over the same period on the standalone basis [27]. Inventory and receivables each rose about 30%, close to the 28.6% revenue growth for the half, and the cash line shows what carrying that build costs.

Receivables were already slow before the first half. The Exencial analysis puts receivable days at 142 in FY2024 and 158 in FY2025 [32], while the snapshot shows 182 and 178 for the same years. The sources disagree on the direction, but both put collection periods between about 140 and 190 days across the record. A supplier whose customers are large OEMs and export buyers can expect long collection periods, and the record shows no sustained improvement.

Debtor days of 189 in FY2026 on ₹603 crore of sales imply receivables of about ₹312 crore, close to the ₹309.2 crore of standalone receivables reported for March 2026 [26]. The day count and the reported balance point to the same level, so the receivables build is consistent across the two bases.

Over the six years, operating cash flow was negative ₹56 crore against cumulative net profit of ₹329 crore. The first-half FY2027 figures show the lag still growing with revenue, so it is not a one-year event that has already reversed.

Supply is narrow at the input end. The sources name Sunflag and Star Wire as the approved raw-material sources, approved for a few grades [13]. For the grades named, the record shows two approved suppliers, which concentrates input risk in the specialty alloys. The record does not disclose raw-material cost pass-through terms, supplier share or inventory policy, so the inference stops at concentration risk rather than extending to margin effects.

Capacity and capital tell the same story from the other side. The company planned ₹450 crore of capex in FY2026 [12] and spent ₹139.3 crore in the first half of FY2027 [20]. Six facilities totalling 44,800 square metres are now in place [21]. Net debt was ₹423.8 crore at the half-year, 0.26 times equity and 1.6 times annualised EBITDA [18]. The ₹700 crore QIP [19] was raised against that build. The consolidated snapshot shows an FY2026 investing outflow of only ₹71 crore, well below the ₹450 crore plan, and an FY2025 outflow of ₹918 crore. This pass records that gap as unresolved.

On unit economics, management says its share of the customer’s wallet in these categories is about 1 to 1.5% [38]. The group earns ₹37.31 of operating profit per ₹100 of sales, which points to high contribution per rupee once a programme is running. The sources do not give part-level margins or win rates [49], so the economics of a new qualified part cannot be measured from the record. They can be inferred only from the group margin and the cash lag.

Export exposure adds a collection and currency layer on top of the working-capital cycle. With about 92% of FY2025 revenue from exports [31], a large share of receivables is owed by overseas buyers, so collection timing depends on each customer’s payment terms and on the currency in which invoices are settled. The record does not disclose the currency mix or the payment terms, so the exposure can be described but not measured.

On the snapshot’s measure, working-capital days of 304 mean that net working capital equals about ten months of sales, up from negative 11 days in FY2021. The asset base has grown with the cash lag. Fixed assets were ₹779 crore at March 2026, more than the ₹603 crore of FY2026 sales, and reached ₹989 crore by September 2026. Capital work in progress of ₹212 crore at September 2026 means part of the capacity has not yet produced revenue. That supports the growth case, and it also means the cash cost of the build is not yet fully in the figures.

The first-half build is in step with growth rather than ahead of it. Inventory grew about 30% from March to September 2026 and receivables about 30% over the same six months, close to the 28.6% revenue growth for the half [22][25][26]. That is the pattern of a business whose working capital scales with sales. The problem is the base: working capital was already large at March 2026, and proportional growth on a large base keeps the cash lag in place. Each rupee of new sales is still financed before it is collected.

Depreciation is the line that moves most with the build. It rose from ₹6.35 per ₹100 of sales in FY2025 to ₹8.79 in FY2026, so each new facility adds a fixed charge that has to be filled before it earns. The snapshot does not split operating expenses between materials, labour and overheads, so the share of each cost cannot be read from the record. That is the main gap in the unit-economics view, and it limits how far the per-100 figures can be pushed.

The bull reading of distribution is concrete. Exports spread demand across geographies [31][47]. Six dedicated facilities [21] give capacity ready for qualified programmes. The 30-to-48-month approval process [29] protects existing positions once they are won. Wallet share of 1 to 1.5% [38] leaves room to grow inside accounts the company already serves.

The bear reading is equally concrete. Export collection periods and rising receivables add cash cost. Narrow raw-material approvals concentrate sourcing risk [13]. Dedicated capacity raises exposure to any single programme’s slowdown, and the capex ramp has come before the cash it was meant to generate. Each of these is visible in the figures above, not inferred from peers.

Net debt is moderate on the reported ratios, but the cash lag means the debt is funding working capital and capacity rather than paying for itself. Chapter 6 tests whether the lag reverses, using the annual statements in the same consolidated basis.
